title: Building RAG and Agentic Systems
subtitle: Build retrieval-augmented and agentic AI systems that hold up: measured retrieval, hybrid search and re-ranking, tool-using agents with memory and plans, and multi-agent teams that check each other's work.
outcomes: Build RAG pipelines with chunking, embeddings, vector indexes and grounded, cited generation
Measure and improve retrieval with recall@k and MRR, hybrid search, re-ranking and metadata filters
Build tool-using agents with validated inputs, retries, approval gates and loop budgets
Give agents short-term and long-term memory, and plans they validate and repair
Design multi-agent systems with typed hand-offs, orchestration and peer review
Diagnose RAG and agent failures from traces and evaluation results
prerequisites: Engineering with Foundation Models, and Prompting and LLM Application Design, whose RAG and ReAct basics this course builds on; Vector Databases and Semantic Search helps with module 1. Install Python 3.10+ and pip install numpy scikit-learn pydantic anthropic (sentence-transformers is optional and downloads small models). Labs run without an API key; their live steps and the capstone need a Claude Console API key with credit and CLAUDE_MODEL set to a current model ID.
description:
Retrieval-augmented generation and agents are how language models get to work on real knowledge and real tasks, and how they most often fail in production: the right passage isn't retrieved, a tool is called with invented arguments, an agent loops until the budget runs out, or one agent's mistake is repeated confidently by the next. This course builds both kinds of system from the parts up, measuring each part as you go. You'll index a handbook and measure retrieval with recall@k and MRR, compare exact and approximate vector search, then improve retrieval with chunking, BM25, hybrid fusion, re-ranking and metadata filters. You'll build an agent loop that validates inputs, retries what's safe to retry, asks before acting and stops itself; give agents memory and plans they check and repair; and finish with a researcher, writer and reviewer team that won't sign off an unsupported sentence.

The labs run on a laptop without an API key, on recorded model turns, so every check is exact, and each has live steps for the Claude API and optional steps with open embedding and re-ranking models. The capstone is an autonomous research assistant: a Researcher agent that calls retrieval and web search tools, and a Writer that turns its notes into a cited report.

modules.title: RAG Fundamentals
modules.summary: How retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model in a knowledge base: the indexing and query pipelines, embeddings and vector search, exact and approximate indexes, and why answer quality depends on retrieval quality.

lessons.title: The RAG architecture: indexing and query time
objectives: Describe the indexing and query pipelines of a RAG system
Explain what RAG offers over relying on a model's training data
key_points: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a retriever, which finds passages relevant to a question in a knowledge base, with a generative model, which answers from them; the name comes from a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues that paired a neural retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator.
Indexing happens ahead of time: load and clean documents, split them into chunks, embed or index each chunk, and store it with its text, ID and metadata such as source, date and access rights.

At query time the system embeds or parses the question, retrieves the top chunks, optionally re-ranks and filters them, assembles a prompt with numbered sources, and generates an answer with citations.
RAG keeps knowledge outside the model, so updating a document updates the answers without retraining, and private or recent information can be used and cited.
Each stage can fail on its own, so log what was retrieved for every answer: a wrong answer is either a retrieval miss or a generation error, and they need different fixes.

lessons.title: Embeddings and semantic search
objectives: Explain how embeddings support semantic search
Compare dense retrieval with keyword retrieval
key_points: An embedding model maps text to a dense vector so that texts with similar meanings lie close together; closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity, the dot product of length-normalised vectors.

Bi-encoder retrieval embeds the documents once, ahead of time, and only the query at search time, which makes it fast; the same model must embed both, and some models expect prefixes, such as 'query: ' and 'passage: ' for the E5 family.

Dense retrieval finds paraphrases that keyword search misses, such as 'live alone' for 'the only adult in your home', but can miss exact identifiers, codes and rare names, which keyword search handles well.
Choose an embedding model for your languages and domain and evaluate it on your own queries; its dimensions, speed and cost matter at scale, and changing the model means re-embedding the corpus.

Latent semantic analysis (LSA), reducing a TF-IDF matrix with SVD, also gives dense vectors, but it only knows words that appear in your corpus, so it can't bridge to new vocabulary as a pretrained model can.

lessons.title: Vector databases and approximate search
objectives: Explain how approximate nearest-neighbour indexes trade recall for speed
Choose and tune a vector store for an application
key_points: Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector: perfectly accurate, but its cost grows with the collection. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes give up a little recall for far less work.

IVF indexes cluster the vectors with k-means and search only the nprobe clusters nearest the query; HNSW builds a layered graph of neighbours and walks it greedily; product quantisation compresses vectors to save memory.
Each index has a recall-speed setting, such as nprobe for IVF or efSearch for HNSW, so measure recall@k against exact search on a sample of queries when choosing its value.

Options range from libraries such as FAISS, through database extensions such as pgvector for PostgreSQL, to dedicated vector databases such as Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Chroma; they differ in filtering, updates, scale and operations.

Store each vector with its chunk's ID, text and metadata, plan for updates and deletions, and record the embedding model and version with the index; Vector Databases and Semantic Search covers indexes in depth.

lessons.title: Retrieval quality limits answer quality
objectives: Measure retrieval with recall@k and mean reciprocal rank
Separate retrieval failures from generation failures
key_points: If the passage with the answer isn't retrieved, the model can only decline or guess, so retrieval quality caps answer quality: measure it on its own with labelled question-passage pairs.

recall@k is the share of questions whose relevant passage is in the top k; mean reciprocal rank (MRR) averages 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant passage, so it rewards putting the answer near the top.
Generation needs its own measures: faithfulness (is every claim supported by the retrieved passages?) and answer relevance (does it answer the question?), checked by people or a validated LLM judge.
Sending more passages raises recall but adds tokens, cost and distraction, so tune the number of chunks with your evaluation set rather than guessing.
Start error analysis from the failures: for each wrong answer, check whether the right passage was retrieved, where it ranked, and whether the model used it.

"""A minimal RAG pipeline over handbook.md: chunk by section, index two ways, measure retrieval, compare exact
and approximate nearest-neighbour search, and build a grounded prompt.

Run: python rag_pipeline.py   (add --live, with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and CLAUDE_MODEL set, to also generate an answer)
"""

import json
import re
import sys

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity


def slug(title):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", title.lower()).strip("-")


def load_chunks(path="handbook.md"):
    """One chunk per ### section, with its ## topic, department and date as metadata."""
    chunks, topic, meta = [], None, {}
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        text = f.read()
    for block in re.split(r"\n(?=#{2,3} )", text):
        lines = block.strip().splitlines()
        if lines[0].startswith("## "):
            topic = lines[0][3:]
            m = re.search(r"department: (\w+); updated: ([\d-]+)", block)
            meta = {"department": m.group(1), "updated": m.group(2)} if m else {}
        elif lines[0].startswith("### "):
            title = lines[0][4:]
            chunks.append({"id": slug(title), "topic": topic, "title": title,
                           "text": " ".join(lines[1:]).strip(), **meta})
    return chunks


class Retriever:
    """TF-IDF (sparse) and LSA (dense: TF-IDF reduced with SVD, a stand-in for an embedding model)."""

    def __init__(self, chunks, dims=12):
        self.chunks = chunks
        docs = [f"{c['topic']}. {c['title']}. {c['text']}" for c in chunks]
        self.tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", sublinear_tf=True)
        self.sparse = self.tfidf.fit_transform(docs)
        self.svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=dims, random_state=0)
        self.dense = self._normalise(self.svd.fit_transform(self.sparse))

    @staticmethod
    def _normalise(m):
        norms = np.linalg.norm(m, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        return m / np.where(norms == 0, 1, norms)  # a query with no known words stays all zeros

    def search(self, question, k=3, method="tfidf"):
        q = self.tfidf.transform([question])
        if method == "tfidf":
            scores = cosine_similarity(q, self.sparse)[0]
        else:
            scores = self.dense @ self._normalise(self.svd.transform(q))[0]
        order = sorted(range(len(self.chunks)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))[:k]
        return [(float(scores[i]), self.chunks[i]) for i in order]


def evaluate(retriever, queries, method, k=3):
    """recall@1, recall@k (the relevant section is in the top k) and mean reciprocal rank (MRR)."""
    hits1 = hitsk = rr = 0.0
    for q in queries:
        ids = [c["id"] for _, c in retriever.search(q["question"], k=len(retriever.chunks), method=method)]
        # TODO 1: find the rank (1-based) of q["relevant"] in ids; add 1 to hits1 if it's first, to hitsk
        #         if it's in the top k, and 1/rank to rr
        pass
    n = len(queries)
    return hits1 / n, hitsk / n, rr / n


def ivf_demo(n=20000, dims=64, clusters=64, k=10, seed=0):
    """Exact search against an IVF index (k-means cells; search only the nprobe nearest cells)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    centres = rng.normal(size=(clusters, dims)) * 0.5  # overlapping clusters, like real embeddings
    data = centres[rng.integers(0, clusters, n)] + rng.normal(size=(n, dims))
    data /= np.linalg.norm(data, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    queries = data[rng.choice(n, 50, replace=False)] + rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=(50, dims))
    exact = np.argsort(-(queries @ data.T), axis=1)[:, :k]
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=clusters, n_init=1, random_state=seed).fit(data)
    for nprobe in (1, 4, 16):
        found, scanned = 0, 0
        for q, truth in zip(queries, exact):
            cells = np.argsort(-(km.cluster_centers_ @ q))[:nprobe]
            members = np.flatnonzero(np.isin(km.labels_, cells))
            scanned += len(members)
            best = members[np.argsort(-(data[members] @ q))[:k]]
            found += len(set(best) & set(truth))
        print(f"IVF nprobe={nprobe:<2}: recall@{k} {found / (k * len(queries)):.2f}, "
              f"vectors scanned per query {scanned / len(queries):.0f} of {n}")


def build_prompt(question, hits):
    sources = "\n".join(f'<source id="{c["id"]}" title="{c["title"]}">{c["text"]}</source>' for _, c in hits)
    return (f"<sources>\n{sources}\n</sources>\n<question>{question}</question>\n"
            "Answer from the sources only, citing source ids in square brackets after each claim. "
            "If they don't answer the question, say so.")


def generate(prompt):
    """The only function that talks to the API."""
    import os

    import anthropic

    client = anthropic.Anthropic()
    reply = client.messages.create(model=os.environ["CLAUDE_MODEL"], max_tokens=1024,
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return "".join(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")


def main():
    chunks = load_chunks()
    with open("queries.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        queries = json.load(f)["queries"]
    print(f"{len(chunks)} chunks; first: {chunks[0]['id']} ({chunks[0]['department']}, updated {chunks[0]['updated']})")
    retriever = Retriever(chunks)
    for method in ("tfidf", "dense"):
        r1, r3, mrr = evaluate(retriever, queries, method)
        print(f"{method:<6} recall@1 {r1:.2f}  recall@3 {r3:.2f}  MRR {mrr:.2f}")
    for qid in ("q05", "q06", "q12"):
        q = next(x for x in queries if x["id"] == qid)
        top = retriever.search(q["question"], 1, "tfidf")[0][1]["id"]
        print(f"{qid} tfidf top hit: {top} (relevant: {q['relevant']})")
    ivf_demo()
    question = queries[7]["question"]
    prompt = build_prompt(question, retriever.search(question, 3))
    print(prompt.splitlines()[1][:110] + "...")
    if "--live" in sys.argv:
        print(generate(prompt))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Lanternfield City Council: residents' handbook

Lanternfield is a fictional city; this handbook was written for the course.

## Waste and recycling
<!-- department: environment; updated: 2026-03-01 -->

### Bin collection days
Household waste is collected every week on the same weekday. Grey bins (general waste) and blue bins (recycling) are emptied on alternate weeks, and the brown food-waste caddy every week. Put bins out by 7:00 on collection day and take them in by the end of the day. Check your collection day by postcode on the council website.

### What goes in the blue bin
The blue bin takes clean paper, cardboard, glass bottles and jars, food and drink cans, and plastic bottles, tubs and trays. Rinse containers and flatten boxes. Plastic bags, nappies, food waste and textiles must not go in the blue bin: a contaminated bin is tagged and left unemptied.

### Bulky waste collection
Large items such as sofas, mattresses and fridges can be collected for a fee: book online and choose up to five items per collection. Collections take place within 10 working days of booking, and items must be at the kerb by 7:00 on the collection day.

## Parking
<!-- department: transport; updated: 2025-11-15 -->

### Resident parking permits
Residents in a controlled parking zone can apply online for a resident permit for each vehicle registered at their address, up to two per household. You need proof of address and the vehicle's registration document. Permits last 12 months and must be renewed before they expire.

### Visitor parking permits
Each household in a controlled parking zone can buy up to 50 visitor permits a year. A visitor permit covers one vehicle for one day, from 8:00 to 18:30, and is activated in the parking app with the visitor's registration number.

### Parking fines and appeals
If you receive a penalty charge notice, you can pay it at a 50% discount within 14 days, or challenge it online within 28 days, giving your reasons and any photos. The discount period is held while a challenge is considered. If the challenge is rejected, you can appeal to an independent adjudicator.

## Council tax
<!-- department: finance; updated: 2026-04-01 -->

### Paying council tax
Council tax is billed each April and can be paid in 10 monthly instalments from April to January, or in 12 instalments on request. Direct Debit payments can be taken on the 1st, 15th or 28th of the month. Pay online, by phone or at a post office with the barcode on your bill.

### Discounts and exemptions
If you are the only adult in your home, you get a 25% single person discount. Full-time students are exempt and must send a certificate from their place of study. People on a low income can apply for council tax support, which is assessed on household income and savings.

### Moving home
Tell the council within 21 days when you move into, out of or within Lanternfield, giving your moving date and new address. Your bill is recalculated from the moving date, and any overpayment is refunded or moved to your new account.

## Libraries
<!-- department: culture; updated: 2026-06-10 -->

### Library opening hours
The Central Library opens from 9:00 to 20:00 Monday to Friday and from 10:00 to 17:00 on Saturdays. Branch libraries open from 10:00 to 18:00 Tuesday to Saturday. All libraries close on Sundays and public holidays; e-books and audiobooks are available at any time in the library app.

### Borrowing and renewals
Library membership is free. Members can borrow up to 15 items for three weeks and renew each item up to three times online, unless another member has reserved it. There are no fines for returning children's books late.

## Housing repairs
<!-- department: housing; updated: 2026-02-20 -->

### Reporting a repair
Council tenants report repairs online, in the housing app or by phone. Routine repairs, such as a dripping tap or a broken cupboard door, are completed within 20 working days. Tenants get a text message with the appointment date and can rearrange it once.

### Emergency repairs
Emergencies, such as a gas smell, no heating or hot water in winter, flooding or a front door that won't lock, must be reported by phone, day or night. An engineer attends within 4 hours to make the home safe. If you smell gas, leave the property and call the national gas emergency number first.

## Planning
<!-- department: planning; updated: 2025-09-30 -->

### Do I need planning permission?
Many small projects, such as some rear extensions, loft conversions and garden sheds, may not need planning permission, but listed buildings and homes in conservation areas have stricter rules. Use the council's free pre-application advice service if you are unsure, and allow 15 working days for a reply.

### Commenting on a planning application
Anyone can comment on a planning application online during its 21-day consultation period. Comments must be about planning matters, such as design, overlooking or traffic, not property values or private disputes. Comments are published with your name but not your address.

"""Optional: the same retrieval evaluation with a pretrained embedding model instead of LSA.

Needs pip install sentence-transformers, which downloads the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model (about 90 MB) on first run.
Run: python embed_search.py
"""

import json

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

from rag_pipeline import load_chunks

chunks = load_chunks()
with open("queries.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    queries = json.load(f)["queries"]
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
docs = model.encode([f"{c['topic']}. {c['title']}. {c['text']}" for c in chunks], normalize_embeddings=True)
hits1 = hits3 = rr = 0.0
for q in queries:
    scores = docs @ model.encode(q["question"], normalize_embeddings=True)
    ids = [chunks[i]["id"] for i in np.argsort(-scores)]
    rank = ids.index(q["relevant"]) + 1
    hits1, hits3, rr = hits1 + (rank == 1), hits3 + (rank <= 3), rr + 1 / rank
    if q["id"] in ("q05", "q06", "q12"):
        print(f"{q['id']} embedding top hit: {ids[0]}")
n = len(queries)
print(f"embeddings recall@1 {hits1 / n:.2f}  recall@3 {hits3 / n:.2f}  MRR {rr / n:.2f}")

hints: ids holds every chunk ID in ranked order, so ids.index(...) always finds the relevant one.
The IVF figures depend on k-means, which can vary a little between scikit-learn versions; the pattern matters more than the exact numbers.
A query made only of words the corpus never uses gets an all-zero TF-IDF vector, so every chunk scores 0 and the first chunk wins the tie.

modules.title: Advanced Retrieval Techniques
modules.summary: Make retrieval better, and prove it: chunking strategies, BM25 and hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, re-ranking with cross-encoders or LLMs, metadata filters and query transformations.

lessons.title: Chunking strategies
objectives: Compare fixed-size, structure-aware and parent-child chunking
Use contextual headers to make chunks findable
key_points: Chunk size sets the granularity of what's retrieved: small chunks match precisely but can lose the context needed to answer, while large ones keep context but dilute the match and spend tokens on irrelevant text.
Fixed-size chunks, by tokens or words with some overlap, are simple and predictable; structure-aware chunking splits on headings, paragraphs or sentences, so each chunk is one coherent unit.

Contextual headers prepend the document and section titles to each chunk before indexing, so a chunk saying 'Permits last 12 months' is still found for 'parking permits'; Anthropic's contextual retrieval goes further, with a model writing a short context for every chunk.
Parent-child retrieval indexes small chunks for precise matching but sends their larger parent section to the model, combining precision with context.
Keep a table's header with its rows and don't split code blocks; then choose between strategies with recall@k on your own questions.

lessons.title: Hybrid search: keywords plus vectors
objectives: Explain how BM25 scores documents
Combine keyword and dense results with reciprocal rank fusion
key_points: BM25 scores a document by the query terms it contains, weighting rare terms by inverse document frequency, saturating repeated terms through k1 and normalising for length through b; k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75 are common defaults.
Keyword search excels at exact terms such as product codes, names, numbers and jargon; dense search excels at paraphrase, so combining them usually covers more questions than either alone.
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists by adding 1 / (k + rank) for every list an item appears in, with k often 60; it needs no score calibration because it uses only ranks.
Fusion isn't automatically better: blending a strong retriever with a much weaker one can pull the strong one's results down, so choose and weight the methods using your evaluation set.

lessons.title: Re-ranking
objectives: Explain two-stage retrieval with a re-ranker
Compare cross-encoder and LLM re-ranking
key_points: Re-ranking is a second stage: retrieve a generous candidate list cheaply, such as the top 20 to 100, then score each candidate against the query with a more accurate model and keep the best few.

A cross-encoder reads the query and the passage together, so it judges relevance more accurately than comparing separate embeddings, but it must run once per candidate, which is why it re-ranks a short list instead of searching the whole collection.
Options include open cross-encoders trained on the MS MARCO dataset, hosted re-ranking APIs, and an LLM asked to grade each candidate; LLM grading is flexible but slower and more expensive.
Measure the gain with a ranking metric such as MRR or nDCG at the cut-off you send to the model, and check that the added latency fits your budget.

lessons.title: Metadata filters and query transformation
objectives: Filter retrieval by metadata, and enforce permissions with filters
Rewrite, expand and decompose queries when retrieval needs help
key_points: Metadata such as source, department, date, language and access level narrows a search, for example to current finance pages, and enforces permissions: filter on what the user may see before anything reaches the prompt.
Pre-filtering applies the filter before or during the search, so you still get k results; post-filtering the top k of an unfiltered search can leave fewer than k, or none.
Query rewriting uses the conversation to turn a follow-up, such as 'what about for students?', into a standalone query before retrieval.

Multi-query expansion retrieves with several rephrasings and fuses the results; HyDE (Gao and colleagues, 2022) embeds a hypothetical answer written by a model instead of the question; decomposition splits a multi-part question into sub-queries.
Each transformation adds a model call and latency, so add the ones your failure analysis shows you need.

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder, SentenceTransformer

modules.title: Agent Architecture and Tool Use
modules.summary: From answering to acting: what makes a system an agent, how to design tools a model can use well, the agent loop in code, and the error handling that keeps agents reliable.

lessons.title: From workflows to agents
objectives: Explain what makes a system an agent
Decide when an agent is worth its cost over a workflow
key_points: An agent uses an LLM as its reasoning engine in a loop: it decides on an action, such as calling a tool, observes the result and decides again, until the goal is met or it stops.

Workflows follow paths written in code; agents choose their own steps. Agents suit open-ended tasks whose steps can't be predicted, where mistakes can be caught and the extra cost and latency are acceptable.
The building block is an augmented LLM, a model with retrieval, tools and memory; many systems called agents are better built as workflows that call one at fixed points.
Agents trade predictability for flexibility, so start with the simplest design, add autonomy only where it measurably helps, and keep a person in the loop for consequential actions.
An agent's behaviour comes from its model, prompt, tools and environment together, so evaluate whole trajectories, not just final answers: which tools it called, with what inputs, in how many steps.

lessons.title: Function calling and tool design
objectives: Design tools, schemas and results that a model uses correctly
Separate read tools from write tools
key_points: Function calling lets the model request a tool by name with JSON arguments matching the tool's schema; your code runs it and returns the result, so the model can use live data and take actions.
Design tools as you would an API for a new colleague: a clear name, a description of what it does, when to use it and what it returns, and typed parameters with enums, patterns and examples.
Prefer a few well-scoped tools to many overlapping ones, and return concise, structured results with IDs the model can use in later calls, paginating large results instead of dumping them.
Separate reads from writes: reads can be retried and run in parallel, while writes, such as changing a booking or sending a message, should be idempotent where possible and confirmed by the user.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard Anthropic introduced in 2024, lets applications expose tools and data to models through one common interface that many clients understand.

lessons.title: The agent loop in code
objectives: Implement the tool-calling loop with correct message handling
Handle every stop reason an agent can meet
key_points: The loop: send the conversation and tools; when stop_reason is tool_use, append the whole assistant reply, run each tool_use block, and return every result as a tool_result with the matching tool_use_id in one user message; repeat until end_turn.

Handle every stop reason: end_turn is a final answer; max_tokens means the reply was cut off, so a tool call in it may be incomplete; refusal means the model declined; pause_turn, from server-side tools, means send the conversation again so it can continue.
One reply can request several tools; independent read-only calls can run in parallel, but all their results go back together in the next user message.
SDK tool runners, such as the Python SDK's beta tool runner, run this loop for you; write it yourself when you need full control over approvals, logging or retries.
Keep the loop's state explicit (messages, turn count, tool calls and tokens used) so it can be logged, inspected and resumed.

lessons.title: Error handling and reliability
objectives: Validate tool inputs and return errors the model can recover from
Apply retries, budgets, loop detection and approval gates
key_points: Validate every tool input against its schema and business rules before running it, and return failures as tool_result blocks with is_error set and a message saying what to change, so the model can correct itself.
Retry temporary failures, such as timeouts and rate limits, with exponential backoff and a cap, but only for idempotent operations: a retried payment or booking change could happen twice.
Guard against runaway loops with budgets: a maximum number of turns and tool calls, a token or cost limit, a wall-clock timeout, and detection of the same call repeated with the same input.
Gate irreversible or costly actions behind human approval, and design the refusal path: the agent should explain what it wants to do and ask, not look for another way round.
Typical failures are the wrong tool, invented arguments, stopping too early, looping, and obeying instructions hidden in tool output; logging every step makes each of them visible.

modules.title: Planning and Memory in Agents
modules.summary: Give agents memory within a session and across sessions, plans they can check and run in the right order, and the reflection that lets them recover from mistakes.

lessons.title: Short-term memory: managing the context window
objectives: Explain how an agent's context grows and why it must be managed
Trim and summarise history within a token budget
key_points: Short-term memory is the conversation and tool results in the context window: everything the model can see in this session, which grows with every turn and tool result.

As it grows, quality, cost and latency suffer, so manage it: drop or shorten old tool results, summarise earlier turns into a short note, and keep a compact state object with the goal and the decisions so far.
Trim from the oldest end, but keep the system prompt, the current task and anything still needed; the history must still start with a user turn and keep each tool result with its tool call.
Count tokens with the provider's counter rather than character estimates when you're near a limit, and keep the stable prefix unchanged so prompt caching still works.
Some platforms manage this for you, with server-side compaction or context editing that clears old tool results, so check what your API offers before building your own.

lessons.title: Long-term memory across sessions
objectives: Decide what an agent should remember, and how to store it
Recall memories by relevance, recency and importance
key_points: Long-term memory persists between sessions in a store such as SQLite, a key-value database or a vector index, so an agent can remember preferences, past requests and their outcomes.

Decide what to write: stable preferences and facts the user states, decisions and outcomes, not every message; a model can propose memories with an importance score, and code applies the rules about what may be kept.
Recall by combining relevance to the current request, recency (for example decaying with a half-life) and importance; the Generative Agents study (Park and colleagues, 2023) scored memories this way.
Memories go stale or prove wrong, so update or replace them, record where each came from, and let users see and delete what's stored about them.
Treat memory as personal data: store only what's needed, keep it secure, set retention periods, honour deletion requests, and never store secrets such as passwords.

lessons.title: Planning: from goal to steps
objectives: Represent a plan as structured steps with dependencies
Validate a plan and run it in dependency order
key_points: Planning breaks a goal into steps the agent can carry out: plan-and-execute has the model write the whole plan first and then runs it, while ReAct-style agents plan one step at a time as they go.
Write plans as structured output, such as a list of steps, each with an ID, a tool, its arguments and the steps it depends on, so code can check and run them.
Validate a plan before running it: every tool must exist, every dependency must be a real step, there must be no cycles, and costly steps may need approval.
Dependencies form a directed acyclic graph, so a topological sort gives a valid order, and steps whose dependencies are complete can run in parallel batches.
When a step fails or returns something unexpected, re-plan from the current state rather than pushing on with the old plan.

lessons.title: Reflection and self-correction
objectives: Use reflection to improve an agent's next attempt
Keep reflection grounded in external signals and bounded
key_points: Reflection lets an agent critique its own output or trajectory and try again; Reflexion (Shinn and colleagues, 2023) had agents write lessons from failed attempts into memory to improve the next one.
Reflection works best with an external signal, such as a validation error, a failing test or a tool error, rather than the model judging its own work with nothing to check it against.
Feed back specific problems, such as 'step s1 uses unknown tool lookup_postcode', not 'try again', so the model has something definite to fix.
Cap the number of attempts and escalate when they run out: models can repeat a mistake or talk themselves into a worse answer.
Evaluator-optimiser loops, in which one model generates and another critiques against criteria, apply the same idea across agents.

"""Plan-and-execute with reflection: validate a model's plan, explain what's wrong so it can fix it, then run
the steps in dependency order, in parallel batches where possible.

The plans are recorded in plans.json. Run: python planner.py
"""

import json
from graphlib import CycleError, TopologicalSorter


def validate(plan, tools):
    """Return a list of problems: unknown tools, duplicate ids, missing dependencies, and cycles."""
    problems = []
    ids = [s["id"] for s in plan["steps"]]
    if len(ids) != len(set(ids)):
        problems.append("duplicate step ids")
    for s in plan["steps"]:
        if s["tool"] not in tools:
            problems.append(f"{s['id']} uses unknown tool {s['tool']}")
        for d in s["depends_on"]:
            if d not in ids:
                problems.append(f"{s['id']} depends on missing step {d}")
    # TODO 1: build a TopologicalSorter from {step id: its depends_on} and call prepare(); if it raises CycleError,
    #         add "cycle between " + the ids in the cycle (e.args[1]) to problems
    pass
    return problems


def batches(plan):
    """Groups of steps that can run at the same time: every step's dependencies are in earlier groups."""
    sorter = TopologicalSorter({s["id"]: s["depends_on"] for s in plan["steps"]})
    sorter.prepare()
    groups = []
    # TODO 2: while sorter.is_active(): take sorter.get_ready() (sorted, for a stable order), append it to groups
    #         and mark each as done with sorter.done(...)
    pass
    return groups


def reflection_prompt(goal, problems, tools):
    """What goes back to the planner model: the goal, what was wrong, and the rules."""
    return (f"Your plan for '{goal}' can't run: " + "; ".join(problems) + ". Use only these tools: "
            + ", ".join(tools) + ". Every dependency must be an earlier step, with no cycles. Reply with a corrected plan.")


def main():
    with open("plans.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        data = json.load(f)
    for n, plan in enumerate(data["attempts"], 1):
        problems = validate(plan, data["tools"])
        if problems:
            print(f"Plan {n}: {len(problems)} problems: " + "; ".join(problems))
            print("Reflection sent to the planner:", reflection_prompt(data["goal"], problems, data["tools"])[:120] + "...")
            continue
        groups = batches(plan)
        print(f"Plan {n}: valid; runs in {len(groups)} batches: " + " then ".join("+".join(g) for g in groups))
        break


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Long-term memory for an agent, in SQLite: what to store, and how to recall it by relevance, recency and
importance (the scoring Generative Agents used). Run: python memory.py
"""

import re
import sqlite3

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

HALF_LIFE_DAYS = 30
WEIGHTS = {"relevance": 0.5, "recency": 0.3, "importance": 0.2}


def should_remember(text):
    """A stand-in for the model's decision: keep stated preferences and facts about the person, not small talk."""
    return bool(re.search(r"\b(prefer|always|never|please don't|I work|my )", text, re.IGNORECASE))


def open_store():
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")  # use a file path to keep memories between sessions
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE memories (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user TEXT, text TEXT, importance INTEGER, day INTEGER)")
    return db


def recall(db, user, query, today, k=3):
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, text, importance, day FROM memories WHERE user = ?", (user,)).fetchall()
    vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit([r[1] for r in rows] + [query])
    relevance = cosine_similarity(vectorizer.transform([query]), vectorizer.transform([r[1] for r in rows]))[0]
    scored = []
    for (mid, text, importance, day), rel in zip(rows, relevance):
        # TODO 1: recency is 0.5 ** ((today - day) / HALF_LIFE_DAYS); combine relevance, recency and importance / 10
        #         with WEIGHTS into one score
        score = 0.0
        scored.append((round(float(score), 3), mid, text))
    return sorted(scored, reverse=True)[:k]


def main():
    db = open_store()
    said = [  # (day, what the tenant said, importance a model might assign from 1 to 10)
        (0, "Please always text me: don't phone.", 7),
        (40, "I work night shifts, so repair appointments before 13:00 are hard for me.", 8),
        (52, "Lovely weather today!", 1),
        (55, "My kitchen tap has been dripping for a week.", 4),
        (58, "My dog barks at visitors, so knock loudly.", 5),
        (59, "Can you collect my old sofa?", 3),
    ]
    for day, text, importance in said:
        if should_remember(text):
            db.execute("INSERT INTO memories (user, text, importance, day) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                       ("tenant-17", text, importance, day))
    print(f"Stored {db.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM memories').fetchone()[0]} of {len(said)} messages")
    for score, mid, text in recall(db, "tenant-17", "When should we book repair appointments for the dripping tap, and should we phone or text?", today=60):
        print(f"  {score:.3f}  #{mid} {text}")
    deleted = db.execute("DELETE FROM memories WHERE user = ? AND text LIKE ?", ("tenant-17", "%dog%")).rowcount
    print(f"Forget request: deleted {deleted} memory; {db.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM memories').fetchone()[0]} remain")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Short-term memory: keep a conversation inside a token budget by summarising the oldest turns.

Token counts here are a rough estimate (characters / 4); use your provider's token counter for real limits.
Run: python context.py
"""

import math


def estimate_tokens(text):
    return math.ceil(len(text) / 4)


def summarise(messages):
    """The only place a model would be called: offline, a stand-in that keeps each dropped user turn's opening words."""
    return "Earlier in this conversation: " + "; ".join(m["content"].split(":")[0] for m in messages if m["role"] == "user")


def fit_to_budget(messages, budget):
    """Keep the most recent turns that fit, and replace everything older with one summary message."""
    kept, used = [], 0
    # TODO 1: walk messages from the newest backwards, adding each to the front of kept while used plus its
    #         estimate_tokens() stays within budget minus 60 (room for the summary); stop at the first that doesn't fit
    kept = list(messages)
    if kept and kept[0]["role"] == "assistant":  # the history must start with a user turn
        kept = kept[1:]
    dropped = messages[: len(messages) - len(kept)]
    if dropped:
        kept.insert(0, {"role": "user", "content": summarise(dropped)})
    return kept, dropped


def main():
    topics = ["Bin not emptied on Monday", "Blue bin rules for glass", "Bulky waste booking for a sofa",
              "Visitor parking permit for Saturday", "Council tax direct debit date", "Dripping kitchen tap"]
    messages = []
    for t in topics:
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"{t}: can you help, please? I've checked the website and couldn't find it."})
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": f"Of course. Here is what the handbook says about that, with the "
                                                         "steps to follow and who to contact if that doesn't solve it."})
    total = sum(estimate_tokens(m["content"]) for m in messages)
    kept, dropped = fit_to_budget(messages, budget=250)
    print(f"{len(messages)} messages, about {total} tokens; budget 250")
    print(f"Kept {len(kept)} messages (about {sum(estimate_tokens(m['content']) for m in kept)} tokens), "
          f"summarised {len(dropped)}")
    print(kept[0]["content"][:120] + "...")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Multi-Agent Systems
modules.summary: Teams of specialised agents: when several agents beat one, how they hand work to each other, how to orchestrate them, and how debate and peer review catch mistakes before users see them.

lessons.title: When to use several agents
objectives: Explain what multi-agent systems offer and what they cost
Choose an orchestration pattern for a task
key_points: A multi-agent system divides a task among agents with specialised roles, prompts and tools, such as a researcher, a writer and a reviewer, coordinated by an orchestrator or by passing work along a pipeline.
Benefits include focused prompts and tool sets, parallel work on independent subtasks, and separate context windows, so each agent sees only what its job needs.
Costs include many more model calls and tokens, more latency, harder debugging and new failures at every hand-off, so use several agents only when one agent with good tools demonstrably falls short.

Common patterns are orchestrator-workers (a lead agent delegates subtasks and combines the results), sequential pipelines and hierarchies of teams; open group chats between peers are the hardest to control.

lessons.title: Communication protocols and hand-offs
objectives: Design typed messages for hand-offs between agents
Describe shared state, message passing and open agent protocols
key_points: Agents communicate through messages, so define them like an API: a task with its objective, inputs, expected output, permitted tools and limits; a result with its sources and status.
Typed messages, such as dataclasses or JSON schemas, make hand-offs checkable; free-text hand-offs lose details and let misunderstandings spread.
Agents can share state through a common store, sometimes called a blackboard, or pass everything in messages; either way, record which agent produced each piece and from what sources.

Open protocols standardise the plumbing: MCP connects agents to tools and data, and the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, introduced by Google in 2025, defines how agents from different systems exchange tasks and results.
Log every message with its sender, receiver, size and time, so a failed run can be traced to the hand-off where it went wrong.

lessons.title: Orchestration frameworks
objectives: Explain what an orchestration layer does
Decide between plain code and an agent framework
key_points: Orchestration decides which agent runs when, what each receives and when the work is finished; it can be plain code, a state machine or a framework.

Frameworks such as LangGraph (graphs of steps over shared state), CrewAI (role-based crews), AutoGen (conversations between agents) and model providers' agent SDKs handle routing, state, retries and tracing.

Frameworks change quickly and add abstractions to learn and debug, so prototype the flow in plain code and adopt a framework when features such as checkpoints, human-in-the-loop steps or tracing save real effort.
Whatever you use, keep state explicit, make steps resumable from checkpoints, bound every loop and agent with budgets, and trace each run from end to end.

lessons.title: Debate, peer review and failure modes
objectives: Use debate and peer review to improve a multi-agent system's accuracy
Recognise and counter multi-agent failure modes
key_points: In multi-agent debate, several model instances propose answers, read each other's and revise over rounds; Du and colleagues (2023) found this improved factual accuracy and reasoning on several tasks.

Peer review gives a critic agent the job of checking another agent's work against evidence, such as whether every sentence is supported by its cited source, and sends it back with specific problems until it passes or a limit is reached.
Critics work best with different instructions, information or models from the agent they check; agents with the same blind spots tend to agree with each other's mistakes.
Typical failures are errors that spread and grow from agent to agent, conformity, endless delegation or revision loops, duplicated work, details lost in hand-offs and runaway cost.
Counter them with verifiable outputs such as citations, independent checks, budgets and stopping rules for every loop, and escalation to a person when agents can't agree.

"""Ready-made tools for the research assistant capstone: BM25 search over the local reports (the RAG side),
a stand-in web search over web_snapshot.json, and tool definitions to give the Researcher agent.

Run python tools.py to check retrieval on the labelled queries (no API key needed).
"""

import json
import math
import re
from collections import Counter

STOP = set("a an and are as at be by for from has have how in is it of on or that the their them they this to was "
           "were what when which who will with do did does".split())


def tokens(text):
    return [w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower()) if w not in STOP]


class BM25:
    def __init__(self, texts, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
        self.docs = [tokens(t) for t in texts]
        self.k1, self.b = k1, b
        self.avgdl = sum(map(len, self.docs)) / len(self.docs)
        df = Counter(w for d in self.docs for w in set(d))
        self.idf = {w: math.log(1 + (len(self.docs) - f + 0.5) / (f + 0.5)) for w, f in df.items()}

    def search(self, query, k):
        scores = []
        for d in self.docs:
            tf = Counter(d)
            scores.append(sum(self.idf[w] * tf[w] * (self.k1 + 1) / (tf[w] + self.k1 * (1 - self.b + self.b * len(d) / self.avgdl))
                              for w in tokens(query) if w in tf))
        return [(round(s, 3), i) for s, i in sorted(((s, i) for i, s in enumerate(scores)), key=lambda x: (-x[0], x[1]))[:k] if s > 0]


def load(path, key):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return json.load(f)[key]


DOCS = load("corpus.json", "documents")
PAGES = load("web_snapshot.json", "pages")
DOC_INDEX = BM25([f"{d['title']}. {d['text']}" for d in DOCS])
WEB_INDEX = BM25([f"{p['title']}. {p['text']}" for p in PAGES])


def search_reports(query, k=3):
    """Local council reports: the vector-database side of the capstone (BM25 here; swap in embeddings if you like)."""
    return [{"source": DOCS[i]["id"], "title": DOCS[i]["title"], "year": DOCS[i]["year"], "score": s,
             "text": DOCS[i]["text"]} for s, i in DOC_INDEX.search(query, k)]


def web_search(query, k=3):
    """Stands in for a web search API. Results can be about other places: check before using them."""
    return [{"source": PAGES[i]["url"], "title": PAGES[i]["title"], "score": s, "text": PAGES[i]["text"]}
            for s, i in WEB_INDEX.search(query, k)]


TOOL_DEFINITIONS = [
    {"name": "search_reports", "description": "Search Lanternfield council's own reports on heat, trees, roofs, Market "
     "Square, cool spaces and budgets. Use it first for anything about Lanternfield.",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"},
                      "k": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 5}}, "required": ["query"],
                      "additionalProperties": False}},
    {"name": "web_search", "description": "Search the web for general evidence (how cooling measures work) or local news. "
     "Results may be about other towns: only use what is clearly relevant, and cite the URL.",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"],
                      "additionalProperties": False}},
]
TOOLS = {"search_reports": search_reports, "web_search": web_search}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    checks = load("eval_points.json", "retrieval_checks")
    found = 0
    for c in checks:
        ids = [r["source"] for r in search_reports(c["query"])]
        found += c["relevant"] in ids
        print(f"{c['query'][:48]:<48} -> {ids}")
    print(f"recall@3 on the labelled queries: {found}/{len(checks)}")
    print("web_search('Market Square traders'):", [r["source"] for r in web_search("Market Square traders")])

   "text": "Sensors on 40 lamp posts recorded city-centre air temperatures up to 4 °C higher than in Riverside Park on the hottest summer afternoons. The hottest streets were around Market Square and the bus station, both with little shade and dark paving."},

   "text": "The council planted 600 street trees between 2022 and 2025, mostly in residential streets. Mature trees shade pavements and cool the air around them through evaporation. Young trees need watering for their first three summers, and 12% of the new trees died in the dry summer of 2025."},
